source_text: Cum deum hoc gradu expellimus, cui nulla conditio\' tam propria et deo digna quam creatoris testimonium praesignarit, narem contrahentes impudentissimi Marcionitae conuertuntur ad destructionem operum creatoris. \'nimirum\', inquiunt. \'grande opus et dignum deo mundus\'! numquid ergo ereator minime deus? plane deus. ergo nec mundus deo indignus: nihil etenim deus indignum se fecisset, etsi mundum homini.\' non sibi fecit, etsi omne opus inferius est suo artifice. et tamen, si quale quid fecisse indignum est deo, quanto indignius deo est nihil eum omnino fecisse! ** uel indignum, quo posset etiam digniorum auctor sperari. ut ergo aliquid + et de isto huius mundi indigno loquar, cui et apud Graecos ornamenti et cultus, non sordium, nomen est, indignas uidelicet substantias ipsi illi sapientiae professores, de quorum ingeniis omnis haeresis animatur. deos pronuntiauerunt, ut Thales aquam, ut Heraclitus ignem, ut Anaximenes aerem. ut Anaximander uniuersa caelestia, ut Strato caelum et terram, ut Zeno aerem et aetherem, ut Plato sidera, quae genus deorum igneum appellat, cum de mundo, considerando scilicet et magnitudinem et uim et potestatem et honorem et decorem, opem fidem legem singulorum elementorum, quae omnibus gignendis alendis conficiendis reficiendisque conspirant, ut plerique physicorum, formidauerint, [initium ac finem mundo constare] ne substantiae eius, tantae scilicet, minus dei haberentur, quas colunt et Persarum magi et Aegyptiorum hierophantae et Indorum gymnosophistae. ipsa quoque uulgaris superstitio communis idolatriae, cum in simulacris de nominibus et fabulis ueterum mortuorum pudet, ad interpretationem naturalium refugit et dedecus suum ingenio obumbrat, figurans Iouem in substantiam feruidam et Iunonem eius in aeream secundum sonum Graecorum uocabulorum. item Vestam in ignem et Camenas in aquam et Magnam Matrem in terram seminalia demessam, lacertis aratam, lauacris rigatam. sic et, Osiris quod semper sepelitur et in uiuido quaeritur et cum gaudio inuenitur, reciprocarum frugum et uiuidorum elementorum et recidiui anni fidem argumentantur, sicut aridae et ardentis naturae sacramenta leones Mithrae philosophantur. et superiores quidem situ aut statu substantias sufficit facilius deos habitas quam deo indignas. ad humilia deficiam? unus, opinor, de sepibus flosculus, non dico de pratis, una cuiuslibet maris conchula, non dico de rubro, una tetraonis pinnula, taceo de pauo, sordidum artificem pronuntiabit tibi creatorem?
pass_a_gloss: When we drive God out to this extent, to the One for whom no condition is more proper and worthy of God than the testimony of the Creator, the most shameless Marcionites, contracting nausea, turn to the destruction of the works of the Creator. 'Certainly', they say, 'the world is a great work and worthy of God!' Is the Creator, then, not God? Clearly, He is God. Therefore, the world is not unworthy of God: for God would not have made anything unworthy of Himself, even if He made the world for man, not for Himself, although every work is inferior to its craftsman. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made something, how much more unworthy of God is it that He made nothing at all! Or is it unworthy, so that one could even hope for a more worthy author. So, to speak about something even of this unworthy world, which, even among the Greeks, has the name of ornament and cultivation, not of filth, clearly, the substances unworthy of that wisdom, whose professors, from whose minds all heresy is animated, have pronounced gods, such as Thales water, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all celestial things, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and ether, Plato stars, which he calls the fiery kind of gods, when considering the world, and its magnitude, and power, and authority, and honor, and beauty, and the help, faith, law of individual elements, which conspire for all things to be born, nourished, finished, and restored, as most physicists have feared, lest the substances of the world, so great, would be considered less than God, which are worshiped by the Persian magi, and the Egyptian hierophants, and the Indian gymnosophists. Also, the common, vulgar superstition of idolatry, when it is ashamed of the names and stories of ancient dead men in images, takes refuge in the interpretation of natural things and hides its shame with ingenuity, representing Jupiter as a fiery substance, and Juno as an airy one, according to the sound of Greek words. Similarly, Vesta as fire, and the Camenae as water, and the Great Mother as the earth, sown with seeds, plowed with oxen, watered with baths. Thus, Osiris, who is always buried and sought in the living and found with joy, argues for the faith of recurring crops, and living elements, and the recurring year, just as the sacraments of dry and burning nature philosophize about the lions of Mithra. And, indeed, the substances that are superior in position or status are more easily considered as gods than as unworthy of God. Shall I descend to humble things? One small flower, I think, from the hedges, not from the meadows, one small shell from any sea, not from the red one, one small feather of a partridge, I am silent about the peacock, will declare to you a sordid craftsman, the Creator?
pass_b_english: When we push God to this extreme—to the One for whom nothing is more proper or worthy than the testimony that marks Him as Creator—the most shameless Marcionites, recoiling in disgust, turn to demolishing the Creator’s works.

‘Certainly,’ they say, ‘the world is a great work and worthy of God!’ Is the Creator then not God? Clearly He is God. Therefore the world is not unworthy of God: for God would not have made anything unworthy of Himself, even if He made the world for humanity, not for Himself, though every work is inferior to its maker. And yet, if it is unworthy of God to have made something, how much more unworthy is it that He made nothing at all! Or is it unworthy, so that one could even hope for a more worthy author.

So let me speak of something even from this supposedly unworthy world, which even among the Greeks bears the name of ornament and cultivation, not filth. The very substances that the self‑styled professors of wisdom—whose minds animate every heresy—have declared to be gods: Thales called water a god, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all heavenly bodies, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and ether, Plato the stars, which he calls the fiery kind of gods. When they considered the world—its magnitude, power, authority, honor, beauty, and the help, faith, and law of the individual elements that conspire to bring forth, nourish, complete, and restore all things—most physicists feared that the world’s substances, so vast, would be deemed less than God, the very substances worshipped by Persian magi, Egyptian hierophants, and Indian gymnosophists.

Even common, vulgar idolatry, ashamed of the names and myths of ancient dead men in its images, flees to a naturalistic interpretation and masks its disgrace with cleverness: it portrays Jupiter as a fiery substance, Juno as an airy one, following the sound of Greek words; Vesta as fire, the Camenae as water, the Great Mother as earth sown with seed, plowed by oxen, watered by baths. Thus Osiris, who is always buried, sought among the living, and found with joy, testifies to the faith of recurring crops, living elements, and the returning year, just as the rites of dry and burning nature philosophize about the lions of Mithras. And indeed, substances that are higher in position or status are more easily regarded as gods than as unworthy of God. Shall I descend to humble things? A single tiny flower from the hedges—not from the meadows—a single shell from any sea—not from the Red Sea—a single feather of a partridge, I say nothing of the peacock—will declare to you a sordid craftsman, the Creator.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Latin syntax and the theological arguments regarding the Creator and the nature of the world. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Locked Latin. The list of Greek philosophers and their associated elements is correctly rendered. The comparison between the 'substances' (substantias) and the 'sordid craftsman' (sordidum artificem) is preserved.
